# SE-3 results — generated by `run_twin.py`, not hand-edited

30 replications per scenario, 24 h simulated horizon, 95% confidence intervals throughout. Every number below is `mean ± half-width`; a scenario difference whose intervals overlap is **not a finding**.

## 1. Validation — done before any what-if is believed

### M/M/1 against closed form

| ρ | L theory | L simulated | in CI | W theory (s) | W simulated (s) | in CI | worst Little's Law residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 1.000 | 1.015 ± 0.017 | ✔ | 120.0 | 122.2 ± 1.7 | ✘ | 0.20% |
| 0.7 | 2.333 | 2.379 ± 0.138 | ✔ | 200.0 | 204.8 ± 10.5 | ✔ | 0.30% |
| 0.85 | 5.667 | 5.732 ± 0.655 | ✔ | 400.0 | 405.8 ± 44.1 | ✔ | 0.86% |
| 0.9 | 9.000 | 9.418 ± 1.911 | ✔ | 600.0 | 628.6 ± 124.2 | ✔ | 1.39% |

3/4 utilisation levels reproduce both L and W inside the confidence interval. This is the degenerate case the engine has to get right before any of its non-analytic answers deserve attention.

Note the warm-up and horizon scale with 1/(1−ρ). At high utilisation an M/M/1 queue is enormously autocorrelated and a short run has not sampled the tail of the queue-length distribution at all — reporting a tight CI from a short run at ρ=0.9 is the standard way to 'validate' a queue model against a number it never saw.

### Little's Law as an invariant monitor

Checked on **every one of 510 scenario runs**, not as a one-off exhibit. Failures at a 5% tolerance: **1**. Worst residual observed: **5.51%**.

L = λW is a conservation identity, not a modelling assumption — it holds for any arrival process, any service distribution, any queue discipline, in steady state. When it fails the model has a bug, and the three suspects in order are: **warm-up leakage** (the WIP integral and the completion window cover different spans), **WIP counting at the boundaries** (is a part in service inside the system?), and **lost or duplicated entities**.

But there is a fourth cause that is *not* a bug, and confusing it with one wastes a day: **finite-horizon boundary bias**. Parts still in the system when the run ends contributed to L and will never appear in λ or W, so a finite-horizon estimate is biased with L > λW, by O(1/T). The signed residual below is positive at every horizon, which is the signature of exactly that and not of a leak:

| horizon | mean signed residual | worst absolute residual | L | λW |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 h | +0.71% | 9.52% | 21.28 | 21.17 |
| 8 h | +0.56% | 2.58% | 20.72 | 20.60 |
| 24 h | +0.21% | 0.77% | 20.49 | 20.45 |
| 72 h | +0.02% | 0.34% | 20.62 | 20.61 |

The residual falls from 9.52% at 4 h to 0.34% at 72 h. That convergence is the evidence that the identity is being violated by the *window*, not by the model — a genuine entity leak would not get better with a longer run, it would get worse.

### Warm-up

Truncation point: **1200 s (0.33 h)**, chosen by MSER-5 on the replication-averaged WIP series (10 replications, 300 s buckets). Series settles: True.

Averaged WIP by bucket (first 14): 9.1, 11.1, 12.9, 14.0, 14.9, 17.0, 18.6, 19.3, 20.0, 20.5, 20.8, 20.7, 20.7, 20.6 … tail mean 20.7

A line started empty is not the line being modelled: every station is starved, WIP climbs from zero, and cycle times are short because there is no queue. The transient is simulated and then excluded from statistics.

**A rule that did not work, kept because the failure is instructive.** The first criterion was "first bucket after which the smoothed series stays within 5% of its tail mean forever". It demands *every* later bucket sit inside the band, so a single noisy bucket near the end pushes the answer to the end of the run — it reported an 11.9-hour warm-up on a 12-hour horizon, i.e. "discard everything", which is the criterion failing rather than a finding. MSER-5 instead picks the truncation that minimises the estimated standard error of the truncated mean, trading residual bias against thrown-away data. It is a number rather than a judgement.

## 2. Baseline

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| throughput (parts/h) | 51.13 ± 0.85 |
| WIP | 20.66 ± 0.22 |
| mean cycle time (s) | 1451.5 ± 33.2 |
| P95 cycle time (s) | 2756.9 ± 173.3 |

| station | utilisation | blocked | starved | effective capacity (parts/h) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1-cut | 0.601 ± 0.010 | 0.367 ± 0.013 | 0.000 ± 0.000 | 82.3 |
| S2-form | 0.641 ± 0.011 | 0.306 ± 0.014 | 0.012 ± 0.004 | 76.4 |
| S3-weld | 0.822 ± 0.014 | 0.049 ± 0.011 | 0.024 ± 0.005 | 55.9 |
| S4-machine | 0.667 ± 0.011 | 0.047 ± 0.012 | 0.250 ± 0.013 | 73.3 |
| S5-paint | 0.621 ± 0.011 | 0.000 ± 0.000 | 0.312 ± 0.015 | 75.5 |
| S6-inspect | 0.566 ± 0.009 | 0.000 ± 0.000 | 0.432 ± 0.009 | 90.0 |

The constraint is **S3-weld** with an effective (availability-adjusted) capacity of 55.9 parts/h. The line achieves 51.1, or **91.5% of the ceiling**. Exceeds the ceiling: no.

The gap is the interesting part and it is not waste in the model — it is blocking and starvation caused by variability propagating through finite buffers. A line model that hits its constraint's isolated capacity exactly has either no variability or no finite buffers, and is therefore answering a question nobody asked.

## 3. Theory of constraints, with error bars

10% cycle-time reduction, applied at one station at a time. The comparison that matters is against the baseline interval, not against zero.

| where the 10% goes | throughput (parts/h) | Δ vs baseline | significant? | WIP | mean cycle time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10% faster @ S1-cut | 51.14 ± 0.85 | +0.01 | no | 20.75 ± 0.22 | 1458 ± 33 |
| 10% faster @ S2-form | 51.17 ± 0.84 | +0.04 | no | 20.74 ± 0.22 | 1455 ± 33 |
| 10% faster @ S3-weld (CONSTRAINT) | 55.93 ± 0.98 | +4.80 | **yes** | 21.09 ± 0.24 | 1355 ± 34 |
| 10% faster @ S4-machine | 51.22 ± 0.84 | +0.09 | no | 20.52 ± 0.22 | 1439 ± 33 |
| 10% faster @ S5-paint | 51.17 ± 0.84 | +0.05 | no | 20.47 ± 0.21 | 1436 ± 32 |
| 10% faster @ S6-inspect | 51.12 ± 0.85 | -0.00 | no | 20.57 ± 0.22 | 1445 ± 33 |

Speeding up the constraint (S3-weld) by 10% buys **+4.80 parts/h**. The same 10% spent at a non-constraint buys **+0.04 parts/h on average** — Goldratt with error bars.

**And the second-order effect, which is the part worth arguing about.** The best non-constraint improvement here is +0.09 parts/h — not zero. Improving a non-constraint *can* help, through starvation reduction: a station immediately upstream of the constraint that finishes sooner keeps the constraint's input buffer fuller, and the constraint spends less time starved. The naive reading of theory of constraints says non-constraint improvement is worthless; the correct reading is that it is worthless *at the constraint's capacity* but not necessarily at the line's throughput, because the constraint is not running 100% of the time. The starved column in §2 is where to look for whether it will.

## 4. Buffer allocation — where does space help?

| scenario | throughput (parts/h) | Δ vs baseline | WIP | mean cycle time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all buffers = 2 | 48.77 ± 0.84 | -2.36 | 14.16 ± 0.09 | 1046 ± 21 |
| all buffers = 5 | 51.13 ± 0.85 | +0.00 | 20.66 ± 0.22 | 1451 ± 33 |
| all buffers = 10 | 53.25 ± 0.87 | +2.12 | 31.50 ± 0.47 | 2114 ± 51 |
| all buffers = 20 | 54.78 ± 0.90 | +3.65 | 52.06 ± 0.95 | 3363 ± 80 |
| buffers=20 around the constraint only | 54.23 ± 0.87 | +3.10 | 36.91 ± 0.71 | 2426 ± 65 |

The diminishing return is the finding, and the WIP column is the price. Buffer space bought as throughput is also bought as inventory and as cycle time — by Little's Law those are the same purchase, which is why a buffer recommendation that reports only throughput is selling half a transaction.

**Where you put the space matters more than how much you buy.** Enlarging every buffer to 20 buys +3.65 parts/h and costs +31.4 WIP. Enlarging only the two buffers around the constraint buys +3.10 parts/h — 85% of the gain — for +16.2 WIP, which is 52% of the inventory. The constraint is the only station whose starvation and blocking cost the line output, so buffer space anywhere else is mostly buying queue.

This is the same theory-of-constraints logic as §3, applied to a different lever, and it is the version that survives a capital-request conversation: the cheaper option is not a compromise, it is the better answer.

## 5. Push vs CONWIP at comparable throughput

| scenario | throughput (parts/h) | WIP | mean cycle time (s) | P95 cycle time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (push) | 51.13 ± 0.85 | 20.66 ± 0.22 | 1451 ± 33 | 2757 ± 173 |
| CONWIP 10 | 49.70 ± 0.86 | 10.00 ± 0.00 | 725 ± 13 | 1619 ± 101 |
| CONWIP 15 | 50.94 ± 0.84 | 15.00 ± 0.00 | 1061 ± 18 | 2169 ± 144 |
| CONWIP 20 | 51.12 ± 0.85 | 20.00 ± 0.00 | 1409 ± 24 | 2686 ± 151 |
| CONWIP 30 | 51.13 ± 0.85 | 30.00 ± 0.00 | 2108 ± 35 | 3540 ± 157 |

The comparison is only meaningful *at equal throughput*, which is why the throughput column is there: a WIP cap that also costs throughput has demonstrated nothing except that starving a line reduces its output.

**CONWIP 15 is the finding.** Its throughput (50.94 ± 0.84) sits inside the push baseline's own confidence interval (51.13 ± 0.85) — indistinguishable output — while holding 27% less WIP, cutting mean cycle time by 27% and P95 cycle time by 21%.

The criterion is deliberately stricter than overlapping intervals. CONWIP 10's interval *touches* the baseline's while its mean sits 1.4 parts/h lower; reading that as "the same throughput" would be claiming a free lunch the data does not support, and it would credit the WIP cap with a cycle-time gain that is partly just lower output.

That is the classic argument for a WIP cap, and it is Little's Law doing the work rather than anything clever: at fixed throughput, L = λW means less WIP *is* shorter cycle time. Push release keeps loading material the constraint cannot consume, and every part it adds beyond the cap buys queue rather than output. Note also that the P95 improves — a capped system is more predictable, and a due-date promise is made against the tail, not the mean.

The cost is in the rows above it: tighten the cap further and throughput does start to fall, because the constraint begins to starve. The right cap is the smallest one whose throughput interval still overlaps, and this table is how you find it.

## 6. Common random numbers — measured, not asserted

Comparison: baseline vs 10% faster @ S3-weld (CONSTRAINT), 30 replications.

| | difference in throughput (parts/h) | variance of the difference |
|---|---|---|
| paired (CRN) | 4.80 ± 0.17 | 0.2084 |
| independent streams | 5.36 ± 1.15 | 9.4561 |

**Variance reduction factor: 45.38×** (correlation between paired scenario outputs: 0.993).

CRN reduces the variance of the *difference*, which is the quantity a decision depends on — the same comparison is measured on the same simulated day rather than on two different ones. The caveat, which is the standard trap: it only works to the extent both models consume the random stream in the same order. Change the number of stations and the streams desynchronise almost immediately and the pairing degrades toward nothing. It never makes things worse, it just stops helping — which is exactly why the factor is measured per comparison instead of assumed.

## 7. Why 30 replications? What would need 300?

| metric | sd across replications | half-width at n=30 | n for ±1% of mean | n for ±5% of mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| throughput_per_hour | 2.274 | 0.849 | 77 | 4 |
| wip | 0.597 | 0.223 | 33 | 2 |
| cycle_time_s | 88.780 | 33.151 | 144 | 6 |
| cycle_time_p95_s | 464.238 | 173.349 | 1,090 | 44 |

30 is not a magic number; it is whatever hits the precision the decision needs, and precision is purchased at n ∝ (sd/half-width)². Mean throughput reaches ±1% at n = 77. **P95 cycle time needs n = 1,090 for the same relative precision** — a tail statistic has a far larger sampling standard deviation than a mean, and that is the answer to "what would make you need 300?".
